figures.caption: Electricity generated is the Federal Reserve's index of output from US power plants, each month's last twelve months against the twelve before, since a single month swings with the weather; real output is gross domestic product after inflation, each quarter against the same quarter a year before, from the Bureau of Economic Analysis. If building and running data centres were pulling power demand ahead of the rest of the economy, electricity would grow faster than output.

figures.caption: Labour's share is the part of business output paid to workers as wages and benefits (the Bureau of Labor Statistics' index for nonfarm businesses); median real pay is the usual weekly earnings of the middle full-time worker, after inflation. If machines took over work and its income went to their owners, labour's share would fall while output kept rising. Labour's share is also the reading behind the labour-share indicator on this page.

figures.caption: Payroll jobs in private education and health services and in leisure and hospitality, as a share of all US payroll jobs, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics; public schools and hospitals count as government jobs, so they sit only in the total. The two sectors stand in, roughly, for work built on people dealing with people, which some economists expect to be in more demand, and better paid, as machines take on other tasks: that view expects this share to rise. Many such jobs sit in other sectors, and not every job in these two is of that kind.

figures.caption: Average weekly hours paid to all employees in professional and business services, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics: a sector that holds much of the office work most exposed to AI, alongside administrative and waste services. A new tool can first make work more intense before it frees any time, and paid hours falling here would be one sign of time being freed; salaried staff are paid for their contracted hours, so time freed for them would not show.
